q: how does a seed know which way is up
seed knows which way is up
how do seeds know which way to grow
roots grow down shoots grow up
how does a seed know which way is up when growing in soil
a: A seed knows which way is up through a biological mechanism called gravitropism (or geotropism). Inside the seed, specialized cells called statocytes contain dense starch-filled organelles called statoliths (or amyloplasts) that settle to the bottom of the cell in response to gravity. This settling triggers a cascade of chemical signals involving the plant hormone auxin. When a seed is placed in any orientation, the statoliths fall to the lowest side of the statocyte cells, telling the seed which direction is down. The plant hormone auxin then accumulates on the lower side of the root, inhibiting cell elongation there, which causes the root to curve downward. In the shoot (stem), auxin promotes cell elongation, so the shoot curves upward. This differential growth response allows roots to grow downward into the soil (positive gravitropism) and shoots to grow upward toward light (negative gravitropism). The process begins within hours of the seed being exposed to moisture during germination, even in complete darkness. This ensures that no matter how a seed lands in the soil, the roots will grow down and the shoot will grow up. Plant biologists have identified specific genes and proteins involved in this gravity-sensing pathway, including the PIN proteins that transport auxin and the ARG1 protein that helps transduce the gravity signal.
